visuals.title: Weighted average cost of capital (WACC)
visuals.formula: WACC = equity weight × cost of equity + debt weight × cost of debt × (1 − tax rate)
visuals.note: Weights at market value. The discount rate for unlevered free cash flow, which belongs to lenders and shareholders together.

visuals.at: Cost of equity equals the risk-free rate, plus beta times the equity risk premium
visuals.title: Capital asset pricing model (CAPM)
visuals.formula: Cost of equity = risk-free rate + beta × equity risk premium
visuals.note: Risk-free rate: government bond yield in the cash flows' currency. Equity risk premium: the extra return the whole market demands over that bond.

visuals.title: Quiz
visuals.text: Five questions. Answer along on the cards below the transcript, then hear Marco's answers.

quiz.pause_at: Pause here if you want to think it through

questions.q: The risk-free rate is 3%, beta is 1.5 and the equity risk premium is 6%. What's the cost of equity?
questions.explain: 3% + 1.5 × 6% = 12%. Beta multiplies the equity risk premium only, not the risk-free rate, and the risk-free rate is still added on top.
questions.explain_at: Cost of equity equals the risk-free rate, plus beta times the equity risk premium

questions.q: Equity worth 600 costs 10%, debt worth 400 costs 5% before tax, and the tax rate is 20%. What's the WACC?
questions.explain: 60% × 10% = 6%, plus 40% × 4% (5% after 20% tax) = 1.6%: 7.6%. Using the pre-tax 5% gives 8%; a simple average gives 7.5%.
questions.explain_at: Three quarters of ten is seven and a half

questions.q: Why do you use the after-tax cost of debt in the WACC?

options.text: Interest is subtracted in the cash flow
Lenders pay tax on interest they receive
Debt ranks ahead of equity in a default
Interest reduces the company's tax bill

questions.explain: Interest is tax deductible, so debt costs less than its headline rate. The saving goes in the discount rate, not the unlevered cash flow.
questions.explain_at: But interest cuts the tax bill.

questions.q: The discount rate rises from 8% to 10%. Which loses more of its present value?
questions.explain: The rate compounds over every year of waiting: the 100 next year falls about 2%, the 100 in ten years about a sixth. That's why growth companies fell hardest in 2022.
questions.explain_at: Now one hundred arriving in ten years.

questions.q: You're valuing NCC's Industry business with a DCF. Whose beta do you start from?

options.text: NCC's group beta, since it owns it
The buyer's beta, since it pays

questions.explain: The rate has to match the risk of the cash flows being valued, so use listed building materials peers. The risk comes with the asset, not the owner.
questions.explain_at: the rate has to match the risk of the cash flows you're valuing
